commit_message:
[wasm-fx] Move asmjs opcodes aside.

The opcodes chosen for wasm-fx conflict with the internal opcodes for AsmJS.

findings.title: Missing guard in DecodeAsmJsOpcode allows invalid opcode to trigger DCHECK crash
findings.message: The function DecodeAsmJsOpcode uses V8_ASSUME((opcode >> 8) == kAsmJsPrefix) instead of a proper validation check. V8_ASSUME expands to a DCHECK in debug builds, causing a crash when an invalid AsmJs opcode reaches this function. The vulnerability is triggered via read_prefixed_opcode which uses LEB128 decoding: if the attacker supplies the AsmJs prefix byte (0xfa) followed by a LEB128-encoded index > 0xFF but <= 0xFFF, read_prefixed_opcode constructs the opcode as (*pc << 12 | index), whose high 8 bits do NOT equal kAsmJsPrefix (0xfa), violating the DCHECK. Similarly, if the LEB128 index > 0xFFF in validation mode, read_prefixed_opcode returns kExprUnreachable (0), which also fails the check. In release builds, V8_ASSUME with a false condition is undefined behavior for the optimizer, potentially enabling security exploitation. A crafted AsmJS wasm module can reliably trigger this crash.
findings.suggestion: Replace V8_ASSUME with an explicit guard check that calls DecodeError and returns 0 when (opcode >> 8) != kAsmJsPrefix. This ensures malformed bytecode is rejected gracefully rather than triggering an assertion or undefined behavior.

ground_truth.root_cause: When AsmJs opcodes were moved to a new prefix (0xfa) in the refactoring commit 3e7191831b, the new DecodeAsmJsOpcode function was written with V8_ASSUME to assert the opcode prefix rather than validating it. The read_prefixed_opcode function uses LEB128 decoding for the opcode index byte, so a multi-byte LEB128 value (index > 0xFF) produces an opcode with a different bit layout than expected by the ASSUME assertion. The original author assumed V8_ASSUME was a mere optimizer hint, not realizing it also embeds a hard DCHECK in debug builds.
